After spending additional 14 hours in this game, I feel I need to add to this review:
once you 'get' what is GTTOD trying to be, and the direction the game is going - you're going to be hooked. True, as of time of writing, the massive change of direction (Sticks and Stones update) is something that makes game feel sparse, but there's enough content here for at least 10 hours.
What makes it so amazing, is the high skill ceiling, and just an incredible feeling of action once you get good at it.
The game softly nudges you in the direction it wants to be played, by an array of awesome features:
- you can double jump, and if you dash midair - it'll recharge one of your jumps
- enemies lead their aim, so if you don't change directions, you're going to get hiit
- while you wallrun, your damage and range are increased
- every killed enemy charges your 'bullet time' ability
- you can cancel reload animations at specific times for each weapon (after clip is inserted)
- enemies are all different: fast chargers, range shooters, kamikaze, flying kamikaze, heavies, shielded, dodging...

Very soon - you'll be doing things like:
1. wallrunning and headshotting two enemies
2. then jump off the wall, fire shotgun at the head of the guy you're jumping off
3. start reloading shotgun in the air
4. land into a slide and do reload animation cancelling to switch to your handgun
5. slow down time and shoot heads of two more enemies as you slide past them

The feeling of action is absolutely insane!!!
After playing this, I loaded Doom Eternal again, and felt annoyed at how slow everything is!

There's enough different weapons, skills and special weapon upgrades to last you enough to become an addict and wait, like the rest of us, for next updates.

If you like shooters where being stationary or looking for cover means instant death - get this. It takes Doom formula and just, imo,  makes it so much better.


Original review:
Very interesting shooter! Sort of like a mix between Ghost Runner and Doom Eternal, wrapped in cheapo Blood Dragon type of graphics.
Movement is very fast, there's jumping, dashing and wallrunning. You get up to 8 different weapons to carry (gotta unlock slots), two specials, two 'skills' - temp slowdown and full freeze, and then there's upgrades.

While the features seem in place, it is a bit sparse. After playing a bit, you'll notice that the features aren't all tuned properly yet. For example, jumping off a wallrun always feels like I'm not quite going where I want to go. Its not just about getting a feel for it - it feels unintuitive.

It is also a bit unstable - it seems to crash every 10-15 minutes for me, so I am unable to complete even a single run for now.

Its definitely worth the money on the sale for now, and if dev doesn't give up and actually implements everything he's planning and talking about - it'll be one really awesome game.

If you love devlogs and being behind the scenes of a game while it's in development, then GTTOD will be your bread and butter. As a game alone in its current state, it's hard to recommend. Off-Brand

Diving a bit deeper, I originally saw this being played by a YouTuber, the footage looked good, their commentary and recommendation was good, and I thought... movement shooter with some roguelite elements? I can get behind that! So I haphazardly bought the game on a whim, I mean, it's pretty cheap and when it's on sale it's really cheap. Even for an Early Access game.

But it's still really rough around the edges. I think most people, if they're not informed will buy it now and be disappointed (and I think that might be why the Steam rating is at 89% at the time of writing). I look at GTTOD, and think of it more as a promise, that one day, I'll go back through my Steam Library, find this game at its full 1.0(+) release, and have a blast. For players like me, it feels more like I've thrown down money as a pledge, and I'm happy to do so in order to support the project & the dev/s. I love the style, love the concept, hope it all gets realized. This is the main reason why I might recommend it.

Some players might be really into the idea of following this games progress along, and will be happy to know that the main developer is super active in their discord, and takes community feedback very seriously. Some people love seeing behind the curtain of a games development and having opportunities to possibly shape the direction of a game. If that's you, I think you'll love joining this game on its journey and being an active part of that community.

But I don't think the majority of people coming to this game will be in either of those mindsets and I believe for them it might be better to wait for this game to develop a bit more. Some of the games mechanics aren't flushed out entirely. The gunplay feels good enough, but gets stale after awhile, because the game just hasn't developed to that point yet. There is no real goal at the moment besides leveling up your character for marginal starting differences. The view bobbing and overall camera shaking is crazy... You can look through the reviews to find more of these kinds of complaints. GTTOD has potential around every corner, and promise at every horizon... it just might take a while in the oven to get there and it's important to realize that.

I think with all that information you can make an informed purchase. Don't buy into the exceptionally well done marketing or the words of YouTubers... and remember that you're not really buying a game right now... but rather the proof of your belief that the devs can put in the work to make and release a great game someday (with the added bonus of an ever changing alpha version of this game on the side).

GTTOD has a decent foundation. The guns and shooting are responsive and satisfying. The visual design of the game is unique but sadly not for everybody. The soundtrack fits well in here as well. It runs quite well too.

However, the game (in the Early Access) does have a number of flaws that I hope will be addressed when it is fully released:

* Difficulty. It's quite punishing and after a couple of hours of playing I still cannot get past the second level. The enemy shots are very accurate and some melee attacks are way too heavy. No matter how high I jump or dash, I still get hit. It's quite a challenge to "charge up" the door to progress to the next level.

* Visuals. As far as I can remember, first time I turned this game on, I thought that I was smoked something funny. Then I tinkered around with the Settings and managed to make it look "playable" to my eyes. I'd definitely encourage others to tweek the Graphics settings a bit if the default settings aren't pleasing. However, even after setting everything to what felt somewhat comfortable, it's still taxing on my eyes to find my bearings and shoot at enemies. The colours are just way too saturated.

* Parkour. I like the idea of being able to wall run during the combat but not every single time before I make it to the first level. The parkour (especially pressing "Shift" to jump high) is not always consistent and if you fall down, you have to start again. Not really fun.

But this is made by one guy who clearly has passion for the project. This is what early access is all about, supporting creators that have the passion and an excellent idea but not a huge studio backing them. I'm very hopeful for this game and this is a rare occasion where I feel Andrew will actually deliver on what he's envisioned. It might not be finished yet, but GTTOD is a ton of fun already in it's current state and on sale or not I think it is definitely worth checking out. I DO NOT recommend this game (as of right now), however I can't bring myself to click "Not Recommended" due to the obvious amount of hard work the developer continues to pour into this game.

I remember the first time I played GTTOD. I had trouble understanding what the goal was, but the mechanics were there and it was pretty fun. When I played it again 6 months later, it was a completely different game. The primary objective had been changed so I no longer understood what to do, but I could tell the mechanics had been refined and that the game was making progress. When I played it again six months after that, it was once more a completely different game and I had to relearn what I needed to be doing in order to progress. Another 6 months later and you guessed it, everything has changed again and I have no idea how to play the game anymore.

GTTOD doesn't seem to understand exactly what it wants to be. While the core gameplay of extremely fast paced first-person combat with parkour elements has always been a constant, everything else seems to be stuck in a state of flux that leaves me confused each time I come back to the game. Is this a wave shooter? A roguelike? An arcade score attack? Are there bosses? Is there an ending? Can I unlock new weapons or abilities? I have no answers to any of these questions before playing the game.

As of right now, I have no idea what the core gameplay loop is or what my motivation to continue playing is. You shoot enemies, make it to an orange door, shoot enemies around the door until it opens, go through it into a new level, then repeat. It's structured similarly to a roguelike but doesn't have any of the clear progression that traditional roguelikes would have, such as multiple distinct level themes, multiple bosses, and an ending (usually with an option to either roll the credits or loop the run and keep playing). In fact, I would say it doesn't seem to have any progression whatsoever? Everything seems to be unlocked from the beginning (except for starter loadouts which are superfluous) and I don't feel rewarded or any kind of satisfaction for making it through levels.

Another issue is the game's lack of a good tutorial and arbitrary design choices that make it difficult to understand what certain items or abilities do, or even WHAT items or abilities you currently have because their icons aren't distinctive or descriptive. Weapons and items can be purchased from boxes in the environment but the environments are usually so large, the boxes so small, your movement so fast, and the lighting so dim that you often just fly past them (literally) without even registering their existence. This causes multiple problems, for one your gameplay style stagnates because you can't find any of the options to remedy that, and two when you run out of ammunition you're screwed because you simply have no idea where any other weapons are. Perhaps this wouldn't be as big of an issue if levels weren't as dark as they are, but as is every level I've seen (which is only 3 despite making it more than 3 levels) are all essentially pitch black.

I hope this game finds and becomes exactly what it wants to be, and becomes extremely successful. But right now, it's hard to recommend because of how frequently and drastically it feels like it changes, and how unclear the objective or point of the game really is. If at some point you fall in love with GTTOD, who's to say it will remain that way? It might be a completely different game in 6 months...

Okay, so..

I had previously given this game a negative review with a couple hours of testing. The biggest issues stemmed from the movement feeling incredibly inconsistent, as a tiny change in position or momentum could give wildly different results. It didn't help that every level began with a platforming section, leading to too much time being frustrated at falling to my death and simply making me not want to play. I had even played it the day before the March 31st update to give it a shot again.

After this update, I can definitively say I'll be spending a lot of time in this game.

To start, it's clear there's been some substantial improvement to the movement mechanics. I can't put my finger on all of the changes, but whatever they did has made a big difference. It now truly feels like your character will go where you want him to go and I'm no longer annoyed at just trying to get around a level. It's not perfect by any means, but it's getting there. I can actually say I appreciate most of how the movement feels instead of bashing my head on a wall, literally and figuratively. And with better movement it's that much easier to get into the meat of the game.

There's been some other solid improvements too. The combat, looting, and progression had always felt sufficient before, but now they're fantastic. I don't think I could describe it any better than just pointing to the video snippets right there on the steam page and saying to watch those. It is a blast being able to experiment with guns for each playthrough and admire the downright incredible animations and sound design the game has to offer.

All in all, I'm more than please with the update. I've had a single continuous run that lasted longer than all of my previous playtime together, and had fun the whole time doing it. It no longer feels like the game hates you for playing it, and that it actually wants you to experience what it has to offer and get better doing it. If you're a fan of the rogue-like aspect of losing progress after death, randomness, looting, but you want small incremental improvements to your character, with the emphasis being on the skill you build in the game, then you'll enjoy this one.

What would happen if Titanfall and Tron had a steamy night of passion while listening to darksynth and vaporwave? This, probably. Although a more mixed option would be more appropriate for this game, I'd still rather recommend it, as it's an amazing concept that is fun as is and has amazing potential to be a lot more in future. TLDR: gud gem, get it.

The good:
-The movement: to say that it's Titanfall inspired would be an understatement (this applies to the whole game and is in no way a bad thing). There's some sprinklings of Ghostrunner, Doom Eternal and Superhot too. You have a wide variety of options and the movement is super smooth, fast and satisfying. Running around in this game never gets old.
-The guns: there's a lot of them, all of which feel amazing, are superbly precise and are made even better by some outstanding sound design and reload animations. Like seriously, I've seen AAA games do far worse in this department.
-The loadouts: this system gives players a lot of choice on how to start each run and provide a wide variety of playstyles.
-The soundtrack: look at some screenshots. What do you think the game sounds like? Yes, exactly. And it's awesome.

The bad:
-Level design: while not bad, it's not as good as it can be in my opinion. There's more fun things that can be done, especially with all the wacky movement options available
-Enemies: they're alright, but the problem lies in that you are soooooo much faster than all of them. Like, in this game you literally play like a speedrunner most of the time and this leads to you simply blasting past the enemies and running circles around them. They simply can't keep up and that kinda cripples the game and stops it from utilizing its full potential.
-Visibility: related to the previous, because of the visual style chosen (while I do like it a lot) visibility can be an issue. From far enough away, enemies just become this blob of light that's barely distinguishable, some enemies are hard to tell apart at first glance and attacks can blend into stuff too. I would suggest that things should be colour coded, similar to Mirror's Edge or Superhot. For example all enemies are coloured red, all wallrunnable surfaces are green, all edges are blue, the escape door is orange (obviously) and so on. This would make things easier to see. Some more minor gripes are that the pure black surfaces are kind of hard to see. You can't tell where there is a slope or whether you can climb onto or wallrun on something when looking from certain angles. Perhaps more lines to designate this should be present. Also, the fish-eye effect from the FOV is a bit too extreme when you widen it to decent levels. If possible, this should be toned down.
-Bugs: it's an early access indie project, so I can forgive this, the issues aren't too severe either. Andrew also tracks these and does his best to fix them in a timely manner. But they still warrant a mention in a thorough review like this.
-Lack of content: this is the biggest one, easily. For now, all you can do is pass through the few levels available or fight in endless modes in the same arenas. Also a lot of features are not implemented yet. Now, I know this is an early access indie game and I have nothing bad to say about Andrew, he's done an amazing job so far. But there's a lot of stuff still missing and the game is sometimes a hard sell with an IOU sitting in place of so much of the content, merely promising what the game could be but isn't yet. I can only wish Andrew all the best in making this vision a reality

Conclusion:
GTTOD is a weird one. I still recommend it, as it's exceptionally fun and cool. Beware though, there's a lot of missing content and you may face some minor issues. Adjust your expectations accordingly. For what it is, this game is still really fun and exciting and worth a try. While we all wait and pray for Titanfall 3, this game offers some epic single player on demand fun. I also sincerely hope that before that, Andrew can flesh out his project and turn the obvious potential that this game has into a rich and complete experience.

[h1] Get To The Orange Door [/h1]
is an 80's synthwave child of Titanfall 2 and Risk of Rain 2. Meaning, a very fast paced movement shooter with rogue like aspects. GTTOD's movement is very smooth and easy to get used to if you already play movement shooters, the gun play is very nice and feels powerful. Lots of weapons to choose from, from a broken pipe to a full auto shotgun and everything in between.
[b] [Gameplay] [/b]
GTTOD has some pretty smart gameplay mechanics, it rewards skillful play with health and a money bonus.
You spend money on new equipment and weapons. Weapons can be 'pack-a-punched' to give them even more power and/or unique traits. Beating levels gives you a unique currency called 'Jade Vines' which can be used on permanent upgrades to help you repeat the gameplay loop.
[b] [Level/enemy design] [/b]
GTTOD's levels are pretty well designed with lots of secrets, well placed enemy spawns, loot-able containers, and other fun items to interact with.
There is a decent amount of levels that all have their own unique feel to them, which is excellent for this type of game. The enemies are also well designed, from ones with shields that go down from one melee strike, to ones with explosive launchers, all while a crowd of grunts are trying to gun you down. You have to adapt your strategy accordingly to the enemy presence.

[b] [Bugs I've found] [/b]
I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs, only ones that inconvenience you. One I've encountered is a bug that can make a few enemies invisible, which sounds bad, but you can still kill them if you can find them, which you can easily do by looking at where you are getting shot from.
Another bug I've encountered is a glitch that can give an enemy insane amounts of health, which is kinda bad because ammo is a little scarce.
[b] [Early access? you mean abandonware?] [/b]
Well i know early access games are notorious for being abandoned, GTTOD is still receiving support and updates, albeit few and far between because the game is made by a team of one or two people, a valid reason for few updates in my opinion.

[b] TL:DR [/b]
Get To The Orange Door is a pretty decent movement shooter with good mechanics, few issues, and a good gameplay loop. It's not the kinda game you sit down and play for 5 hours, just 'i'll just do a few runs then get off' type of game.

Homemade Vanilla Bean Custard Ice Cream

INGREDIENTS:

1 1/4 cups Heavy Cream
2 1/4 cups Whole Milk
2 Vanilla Beans or 2 teaspoons Pure Vanilla Paste or Extract
3/4 cup Sugar
3 Egg Yolks

INSTRUCTIONS:

To make Custard Base Vanilla Ice Cream (with egg yolks):

Combine the cream, whole milk, and vanilla beans into the medium pot.
Start to heat mixture over low heat.
Whisk the sugar and egg yolks together in a small bowl until fully combined.
When the cream mixture reaches 95 degrees or feels warm to the touch, remove from the heat.
Carefully, add 1/4 of the cream mixture into the yolks, whisking constantly until blended.
Do not add all of the cream mixture at once to the eggs.
You want to slowly add heated cream a little at a time to temper the yolks.
Whisk the tempered yolks into remaining warmed cream mixture.
Return pot to medium-low heat.
Cook the ice cream base over medium low heat until it reaches 185 degrees or is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Remove from heat.
Remove vanilla bean pods and scrape vanilla beans into ice cream or add pure vanilla extract.
Pour ice cream mixture into a bowl to cool.
Fill a large bowl with ice. Place the container of ice cream in the ice bath.
Stir often and let cool.
When the ice cream base has cooled, pour into ice cream machine and churn according to manufacture's instructions.
When finished churning, transfer to airtight container.
Allow ice cream to harden in the freezer for 30 minutes to 1 hour.

Just played the new update, and that is my conclusion after 4 hours with it.

Let me explain. I've been playing GTTOD since back in the day, when the levels were procedurally generated, the graphics were nice but flat, there was no ammo, and holy hell was the grenade launcher op.

It was a decent time killer back then, with really fun mechanics, but not alot more. I really liked the movement (Although i would have played a f*cking hello kitty game if it had wall riding at that point. Jesus was i down bad) but didn't think much more of it. A fun time waster, with fun gunplay.

After not playing the game for a while, i came back just in time for the (appropriately named) Excessively late update.

It was... not what i hoped for.

Don't get me wrong, the game got way better in many ways. Graphically, the game felt like it finally got out of puberty, and was starting to figure out a direction. The guns were more refined, more satisfying, and felt way better to use overall. The enemies were becoming diverse, not just, y'know, a dude and a drone. I had to actually pay attention to who i was fighting, but the enemies were visually distinguishable, so there was no difficulty there. And the music, oh lord, whoever produced it is a genius.

But, as much as all i've said above is great and all, one thing took a noticeable hit. The movement.

It felt incredibly clunky. Instead of feeling like an agile hyper-soldier, outmaneuvering my enemies, i felt like a brick in a space suit. To be more specific, the wall running was sh*t. 

You could be going straight for a wall, after gathering a f*ck-ton of speed, and just straight up face plant into it. And you could say "Well maybe they made it more difficult to be more skill expressive". And i could accept that, if it wasn't for the fact that it felt like i had no control over it. Sometimes i would get sucked to walls that were behind my back, sometimes i'd be hitting the walls at the perfect angle, and my dude would just go "Nah lmao" and fall like a bag of bricks into the f*cking abyss.

Point being, i hated the movement, so i dropped the game.

Now, you can take all i wrote above, and wipe your f*cking ass with it, because the dev decided to seclude himself to the tibetan mountains for 16 months and came back with the best update i've ever seen in my life.

Here i was thinking the guns were good in the last update. Nah. The sound design of each and every gun (i've tested so far) is godlike. The impact of every shot feels incredibly satisfying. The level design is on a whole 'nother level. The enemies, more striking. And while not everyone would agree, i prefer the new music over the old one.

But the movement. The f*cking movement.

Smooth. Fast. Incredibly f*cking addicting. I might as well be playing "the floor is lava"  with how much time i spend not flying through the air. It is, without a doubt, the best movement in any game i played. And f*ck me, i have around 600 hours in titanfall 2.

I could go on for days about it. And hell, that's not even where this update ends, not even close. But i don't wanna write a whole ass paper boosting low_hanging_fruits(the main dev)'s ego, so you'll just have to discover all of it by playing the game yourself. All jokes aside, this update is absolutely incredible, and i cannot recommend enough that you should get the game and try it out for yourself. 

As a last note, i do have to say i'd highly appreciate a waypoint/minimap system, since my ape brain always forgets where all the bunkers are when i have 3 keys.

As someone who has been playing and monitoring development since close to this game's initial release, it has been an incredible experience to watch it grow and evolve. It is crazy fun and the recent updates have really added a sense of progression which is something this game was previously missing. 

TL/DR: This is an incredible, satisfying skill based game that has grown incredibly since launch and will only continue to evolve with players' participation.

This game is INCREDIBLY fun. solid game play loop, fun movement, beautiful areas, and some really sick animations (especially for the guns). however, there are still some pretty big flaws that need to be addressed for this game to really stand out.

1. There is little to no build variety to runs. blessings matter very little when 1 babe'd gun can carry you to threat 50+ easily. and the blessings don't feel super unique. more health, more resources, explosion on kill if the enemy is burning. there are very few synergies between them that make them feel boring. 

a random idea i had was keeping the blessings at the end of the level (Similar to Gunfire Reborn's end of stage chalice) and giving the bunkers something like relics or artifacts (EX: something like slay the spire's relics or Enter the Gungon's passives where they give a buff that is active at all times) giving each their own sort of purpose. something like a shoulder missile launcher attachment that gives a chance to fire a homing rocket when an enemy is hit with non elemental weapons or sliding leaves behind flammable oil that can be ignited to make a wall of fire (effectively an AOE DoT). they all dont have to be super unique, some can just be damage or reload buffs, but more ways to scale yourself in a run can really add to the replayability.

2. The curses are REALLY COOL. the curses are done incredibly well with some EXTREMELY fun combos with weapons and even between themselves. some standout ones being: 2 skulls that home onto people you shoot, re rolling your guns every threat level (complete chaos LMAO), launching ice spikes that can hurt you by freezing already frozen enemies, enemies who die spawn as a phantom that explode into frost when killed but will revive if not killed quickly. 

3. bunkers feel empty and keys drop far too often. the bunkers are probably the most "unfinished" feeling part of the game with one bunker layout just straight up having a message saying "tee hee sorry not done yet" (which is really funny honestly). something i would love to see is more straightforward bunker types, stuff like the arsenal bunker and the cargo tunnel bunker with ways to tell what a bunker is by just looking at it (EX: blessing bunkers have vines overtaking the door, arsenal bunker having a heavily armored door, cargo tunnel bunker looking worn down and abandoned from the outside with rust covering the door and a crooked light above it, alpha cash bunkers having a shiny golden door) so players can make choices that can impact their run.

4. the clothing system in general. incredibly restrictive and most being not very impactful to your build. there are very few options in the pool as well. HOWEVER, i would love to see a system similar to BPM's where you have 4 slots (1 head, 1 glove, 1 chest, 1 boots) allowing for combos, but still being restrictive enough for there to be an important choice with what you take and leave.

5. the hub. its empty and has very little to do other than leave. something to make the harbor feel more lively is maybe something like how Hades handles its hub. i know that this game is gonna be pretty heavy with story in 1.0, though maybe sometimes seven, eight or nine could drop by the harbor from time to time and have a bit of dialog. dialog between six and the mother when you spend jade vines to level up. maybe the mother could give you some encouragement when you start a run (similar to Hades where Hades just insults you) small bits of world building do wonders for keeping people interested in the world. though, i dont really know where the story is going (i read the wiki for a bit) so maybe this wouldn't fit thematically

at the end of the day, i would love to see more replayability and unique synergies with items. most of this has been me just spit balling ideas (take them with a grain of salt(i am NOT a game dev)) that i think would add to runs. nothing is meant to insult, its just some criticism of some of the systems. i am very excited to see where the game is going to go from here, it has a LOT of potential to be amazing.

So! Get To The Orange Door just obtained a massive update and so I'm going to write a review for the game. I'll go over what I liked and what I didn't like.

Like: 

Everything great and fantastic about the previous version of the game (which is still accessible - Thanks, Andrew!), has been tweaked, reworked and incidentally - vastly improved. Controls are much more fluid and responsive, the shooting feels fantastic and the levels went from great to [i]Legendary[/i]. Honestly, if this was it, I'd recommend that the Developer raise his price or he'd be giving money away.

For bosses, I haven't run into the Legion Sentinel yet, but the Blade Sentinel has become an actual challenge, with a real boss arena that rewards outmaneuvering him as well as outgunning him. Since the previous arena was a couple of raised platforms, this is a major improvement and I'm excited to see where he goes for boss fights next!

Last, and certainly not least, the removal of the platforming sections at the start of every run. Normally, first person platforming doesn't bother me in the least, but I always managed to trigger some bug or cause an issue with the movement that made completing the segment either harder than it should've been, or outright impossible thanks to a bug that was impossible to fix.

Dislike:

The main draw of this update is the dungeons and...they're very basic. It's basically a railroad of the same set of rooms arranged randomly. Mostly, it's combat encounters that you clear, then move to the next area. This wouldn't be too bad, if not for two things that make compound to make this problem worse than it should be.

The first is that the game's difficulty has spiked considerably. This is both to due with the enemy's improved AI over the last version, but also to do with the Player's capabilities being reduced to make room for the Meta Progression System.

The second is that the Dungeon's are the fastest and most efficient way to obtain Jade Vines, the currency required to progress through the Meta Progression System. Which means that, if normal runs are giving you trouble and are nearly unbeatable, you wind up, as I did, grinding dungeons for several hours until you've progressed to the point where you've got a couple of extra lives, starting bits, etc...which means you're traversing the same set of 3-4 rooms with combat encounters for [i]hours[/i] just to be able to attempt a normal run. Considering that these rooms are not nearly the same quality as the massively reworked levels of the main runs, this...is not a good thing.

Also, I dislike dual-wielding. Not the concept, but the implementation. For your guns, you click the left mouse button to shoot the gun in your left hand and the right mouse button to shoot the button in your right hand. Now, in a controller, I imagine it feels a lot more natural, but on a Mouse and Keyboard, it just felt awkward. Also, when you reload your guns, you briefly hold onto the first gun with both hands for a second and then reload the second...and then briefly hold onto the second gun for a second before slowly bringing up the first gun. Kind of unnecessarily slows down dual-wielding's combat.

Fixes: I don't want to just cry and say 'these things are bad' because, while I dislike them, they aren't game breaking and, if the developer would care to listen, here's some fixes I think may alleviate the problems.

For the Dungeons, I think you want to focus on the two problems that compound. Number 1 is varying up the dungeon rooms, which I'm sure was going to be done anyway. I would like to see more than one exit to every room (similar to Hades) so that a bit of player choice is preserved.

Also, the difficulty I believe should be re-balanced to allow those who aren't godlike at shooters a chance to complete normal runs without feeling pressured to grind several hours of dungeons first. I understand this is already being done, so please take this as a word of encouragement.

Finally, for dual-wielding (specifically semi-autos), as much as it's cool to be able to fire one gun for a bit, then fire another gun, or fire both at the same time, I think expediency and automation would be a fine trade for a little bit of player expression: While dual-wielding semi-auto firearms, have the main firing mode be firing them one at a time, then have the secondary fire-mode be shooting them simultaneously.

For automatic firearms, I don't think any change is necessary, or if you have an auto in one hand and a semi in the other. Just while dual-wielding semi-autos. Also, please adjust the reload animations. Thank you!

Conclusion:

I've always been in love with movement shooters and just fast paced FPS games in general, Quake and Titanfall were and still are the games I'd point to for my fascination with this genre. I've followed GTTOD's development and finally decided to try the game myself and shell out the cash, and needless to say given the current state of the game I'm not disappointed. 

This gameplay scratches that itch of the niche that I love, the movement is sleek and quick and the gameplay, although somewhat tedious given the lack of enemy types ranging from cannon fodder to a slight threat still gives you that adrenaline filled rush of slide hopping and air strafing combat constantly. While the average player new to the movement shooter niche might struggle for me the game felt immediately responsive. Not to mention the art style and design is top notch. Every weapon feels powerful and tailored in design and gameplay to a mark.

But enough about me praising the game, lets go over some issues that I have encountered and would like to make anyone reading this aware of.

Glitches and bugs, while the game for being early access is expected to have bugs it should be noted that you will eventually run into something that will ruin your run. For me I lost my 10k kills run due to entering the battle portal a second time believing it was something new to find a weapon or piece of content, instead it resulted to softlocking my run and forcing me to restart, in all honesty I was quite livid to losing my run and therefore progress to the achievement but its to be expected. I can easily break the record of where I left off, but I'd prefer to not have to worry about my time being turned to naught. Any other glitch you may encounter tends to be quickly remedied and doesn't harm you, I just was particularly unfortunate in the timing. But to to the fact it was present and finding that I'd consistently phase into walls in some occasions due to the sheer speed I was propelling myself with slide hops I don't doubt for a fact that the issues are still greatly present. It is early access and I can fully understand if these are present, but it is something to be aware of when purchasing.

Content, at the time of writing the game is quite small given the 15 dollar price tag, its quite fun however unless you are like me, a person who can't seem to fill their addiction to anything fast paced then I must be blunt and say to consider your purchase carefully. It is a fun game, but until it gets more content outside of around a half a dozen levels I can't give a 100% recommendation in good faith to anyone who isn't fluent in the genre.

Graphics, the default bloom is, to put this rather bluntly hard on the eyes, after a hour of gameplay I had to turn it down to half of default due to it harming my target acquisition. However everything else is perfectly fine.

Those are the issues that come off the top of my head, I've greatly enjoyed the game and looking forward to the continued development of GTTOD.

Quick and simple: 9/10, far improved from what it used to be. 

Complicated answer:
If you were turned off from GTTOD in the past, due to jank, lack of progression, or a artstyle that didn't have much direction, but were really into the concepts at play, well have I got news for you. The game is in the best state it's ever been in, with quickplay (a simpler, clear a floor, move on mode with no progression saving) and the main gamemode being fleshed out (finally), I can confidently recommend this game now. The kinks have been (mostly) ironed out, it's better optimized, and the visuals are so much better.

Gameplay/Movement:
The gameplay is smooth and fluid, and immensely satisfying, and entirely skill based, even with maxed out grenade launcher, if you get too cocky, you'll get killed quick. With the most recent updates, having overhauled blessings and curses, along with adding clothing for additional effects, you can build classes, everything from a, one hit wonder, doing insane damage, but with no health, or a juggernaut that heals on every kill, with classes often slipping into different types, depending on what weapons/equipment you have, or your skill level.

Maps/Levels:
The maps in this game are linear, you have a set path, and you follow it till the end, where you go on to the next map. The entire game is like playing the TF|2 gauntlet mode, but if the enemies fought back. Speeding through the levels is addicting, get faster and faster times, as you progress and become more skilled, it's like a neon-gun filled acid trip, and I love it. (I swear I can stop anytime I want).

Visuals/Design:
(somewhat) recently the shaders got a overhaul, drastically improving FPS, and looks. And it certainly looks. You'd have to be blind not to see this game. It's like if you took the neon-dipped aesthetics of Hotline Miami, the weapons and enemies of Halo and DOOM, the movement of TitanFall2 and put them into a blender with just a hint of some "snow" and essence roguelite, you'd get GTTOD.

Mods:
The game is moddable via the steam workshop. Not much there now, but what's there is some good stuff, you can add/change music, weapons, and more, and I'm sure we'll see some of those "other" mods as the game gets more popular.

P.S: Thanks Andrew for your hard work, if you see this, you've probly made the best movement game on the market right now, and I'm grateful to you for fueling my speed addiction (i can stop anytime i want)

I've tried this game twice now and I still can't recommend it.

The art style is unique but misses the mark, ending up as seizure inducing rather than unique. Please, use any colour other than pure black for the world and it will do wonders for the art style in an instant. There isn't enough manual direction over the neon and black only style for it to look good. It would also be nice to have an option to turn down the bloom instead of just off, which also seems to erase 90% of the colour from the world aswell.

The moment-to-moment gameplay is fun and engaging, and the music is phenomenal, but the feedback for making mistakes and enemies hitting you is garbage. Melee enemies seem to have go-go-gadget extendo arms once you exist near them for a milisecond, and enemies themselves and enemy projectiles have are hard to visually acquire because they're being drowned out by the bloom, projectiles are completely inaudible, too small, and way too fast, and enemies all make the same noise and have no footsteps. Taking damage constantly for no reason because an enemy who is as fast as me was next to me briefly is not fun at all, and the game doesn't even make an effort to notify me that I've taken damage.
And several times now I've been clipped by a melee and one shot through shields. 
I cannot stress enough that shield gating is NON NEGOTIABLE in games like this. Not only does it cut player frustration infinitely, it also allows designers to create more engaging enemies that do cooler things because they don't have to be worried about the player dying through 1 shield/1 hp to like some puddle on the ground they can't see.

The guns are very satisfying to use, and I appreciate the great amount of effort that's been put into them. Even taking into account the bloom kind of blowing everything up, they still look (and feel) great.
While it's fun, I think player melee is actually a little bit too strong the second you come out of the gates. In a first person shooter, I'm not expecting my fist to do more damage to the hordes of polygonal nerds running at me than an actual firearm, but this guy is apparently a default fighting game character and wall splatting enemies like crazy. Again, fun, and it works, just a little out of place in my opinion.

All in all, I think if this game got a major visual overhaul and a sizeable gameplay overhaul, it would be a strong contender for sure, but not in its current state. However the fact that the devs have come as far as they have since I personally last played is still considerably impressive, and I'm really hoping the game is able to improve to the point where I start seeing tiktok edits of it. I love the cover art for the character and I need to see people make videos of the dude.

I didn't make it out of the introductory level/tutorial.

Okay, well, the best place to start is at the beginning.

There's an unskippable cutscene at the beginning, and not a very short one, either. That's a little annoying, but it doesn't bother me as much as some people, as many games that really want you to understand their story will make the opening cutscene unskippable the first time the player sees it so as to make sure they understand the setting.

So the deep and intricate story of "guy crashes his ship somewhere" unfolds, and the first thing you might notice is that the camera moves around like a greased meerkat on espresso. 

You're gonna wanna turn down the sensitivity, because the next jumping sections are unpleasant, particularly the ones where you have to wall jump. See, you need to stay parallel to the wall in the wall-running segments and the camera moving wildly every time you nudge the mouse doesn't help. 

Once in a while, though you will fall off the wall for some reason likely due to shifting the mouse slightly. Also once in a while you will also BOUNCE OFF THE WALL LIKE A SUPERBALL OR GET SHOVED OFF A LEDGE BY HAWLEY GRIFFIN APPARENTLY WHY GOD WHY 

But also sometimes you kind of float vaguely toward a ledge and either land or get lost in the architecture. It's very pretty architecture, but there's no way out of it.

So, in most games when you screw up a part of the tutorial, you repeat that part. 

There are no checkpoints in this tutorial. In THIS game, if you screw up the jumping parts of the tutorial you get sent back to the very first screen of the tutorial and get to walk through everywhere you've already been. Thankfully, everything you've opened or collected remains in your inventory, but it still an irritating slog back to where you were.

Particularly since the ability to do things like dash or double-jump are locked until the player reaches that section even if the player knows how to use them already. 

But at least you don't die from falling off a ledge, you just lose a bunch of hit points. For now.

Once you manage to get past the jumping parts, you actually get into the intended combat tutorial.

There are visual differences between the robots. I honestly can't tell if that means different abilities, because the robots all immediately detected my presence once I reached a certain distance from them whether they had line of sight to me or not and came for me. 

I'll be the first to admit that FPS games aren't my favorite genre, but if the very first enemies encountered in an FPS game walked or ran normally then instantly zoomed--POOF--into the players face once they closed in to a certain distance and started attacking instead of transversing the distance as they had been, I don't think anyone else would enjoy them either.

If the robots walked normally and started running somewhat faster when they get close enough, that would make sense. If a specific enemy class did this, sure, keep an eye out for them. Here, the grunt enemies reach say, twenty feet from you, and BAM in your face.

One time I backed myself off a ledge trying to get away from three or four in my face at once. And died, because all of a sudden falling off a ledge was fatal.

The robots don't all look the same but I couldn't tell if they had different abilities. Because they were in my face instantly and that's pretty much all they needed. 

Also, there's no radar or any way of telling if the robots are behind you until you're attacked.

So, I got killed in the tutorial, and I mentioned how messing up jumps in the first part of the tutorial takes you all the way back to the beginning spot of the tutorial, yes? Well, actually getting KILLED in the tutorial takes you...

ALL THE WAY BACK TO THE BEGINNING OF THE GAME.

RIGHT TO THE START OF THE UNSKIPPABLE OPENING CUTSCENE.

Is it skippable THIS time?

NOPE.

I hit space, and return and ESC and tried every button on my mouse, and nothing.

So every time the robots, who I should say again, INSTANTLY get in your face and attack from further away than you would like, wreck you in the tutorial, or if you back up too far trying to get away from them and fall off a ledge back to the beginning you go, and the not-very-short cutscene seems unbearably long the third time or so you see it.

I look at the trailers and I see a lot of jumping and bouncing and shooting. I see a bunch of cool, interesting levels that look fun to explore and travel through and fight things in, maybe with interesting secrets or fun tricks.

I play the game and I get frustrating wallruns and floaty jumps, weird physics, vaguely interesting stuff going on in the background really far away, enemies who don't seem to have any attack patterns or variety, except when they're lunging at me like they had rockets in their backsides.

Maybe the main game is like the trailer, but if the tutorial makes me want to play something else, how am I ever going to know?

I acknowledge that the development team is very small, and doing the best they can. The most recent news they posted mentioned the difficulty they had with getting the tutorial off the ground, but I honestly believe that the game as  a whole needed more playtesting and quality-of-life improvements before even being released as EA.

Right now on 8/7/2023, I can't recommend this game. If I'm still alive in a year or so, I might give it another whirl, but it's gonna be a bit before I feel like seeing the opening cutscene again.

To start off with, the pros:

- The game is beautiful. It looks straight out of TRON or whatever other synthwave/outlast wet dream you can think of.
- The sound design is stellar. All of the guns that I've played around with so far are beautifully designed from shooting to reloading.
- The animations are amazing and easily some of the best in the industry. I'm especially fond of the pistol, especially the draw animation.
- The time slowdown feels orgasmic. It's so fun to use.

Onto the cons:

- Some parts of the game are so, so, so slow. For instance, there's one objective where you have to kill a certain number of enemies while inside an arena to build the door. The problem is that the enemies barely come and you can't exit the arena to search for them. 
- It's pretty demanding. I was able to run it fine but lower-end systems are gonna feel the burn.
- There's not a lot of enemies. There's drones, suicide bombers, enemies with shields, enemies with swords, projectile throwers, fodder, and... that's it, really. Compared to other shoot-em-ups like ULTRAKILL or -- dare I say it -- DOOM Eternal there's a lot to be desired.

So, I really wanted to like this game and it really appealed to me, the synthwave tunes and the new retro design are amazing. The guns are snappy and its somewhat fun to shoot them and yet the lack of ammo and the short magazines break up the pace of the game.

But the biggest disappointment for me was the parkour mechanics that are really really bad, even the wall-running was consistently failing. The movement speed is fast but feels really sluggish and its hard to properly execute the movements you have in mind as there is 0 inertia in this game.

The way you jump off walls gives you a strong boost in the opposite direction of the wall, which really takes away the players freedom of moving the way they want. Also the dash mechanic is counter-intuitive as it will slow you straight away after the dashing... 

All in all the game looks amazing and has as mentioned snappy guns that are fun to play with but this is sadly sabotaged by restricting and broken movement mechanics.... 
Which IMHO is the games biggest appeal apart from its aesthetic design and snappy gun-play. 

I wish the developer best of luck in improving the game in these aspects as the game has great potential to become something great. So far it is already a nice game and I will keep an eye on it for future updates but until then I will have to get a refund for the game, sadly...

GTTOD is a buggy mess that is more frustrating than fun to play. Wall running is clunky, and massively over simplified. It is incredibly sticky, while at the same time, juxtaposing itself by being not sticky enough. I can jump up to a wall that I would like to run on, and bounce on it for a while until my character decides "yup its time to run on this baby" or "nope you're going to fall" and either die, or land back on the ground. At the SAME TIME, I could be running along a wall, transition to a new wall, and get stuck to a completely different wall because my character magnetized to it first, instead of going to my intended target. Sometimes when I do get my character to initially jump on the right wall, they will go through the wall to either stick to something else or fall to their death. Its frustrating, its annoying, its not fun. 

Shooting feels mediocre at best. Killing robotic enemies over and over is unsatisfying, seeing their new forms can be confusing, and honestly, if you fly through the level the enemies are skippable anyway (which is also, too easy to do). 

Walking up ramps can sometimes see you get stuck in the floor, or move through the floor so that you have to move a certain way to get yourself out of the floor. This is death in a movement game. Not by enemies, but by mechanics. Its annoying. It's not fun.

I have no idea how this game is so highly recommended. I'm not going to comment on anybodies fun, if you're someone who is having fun with it, great, continue to do so. Small developers need all the support they can get. That being said, this game is an un-enjoyable mess at this point. 

The music and presentation are pretty cool. Nothing earth shattering, but the game is good to look at, and the music pumps energy into what you're doing. 

All in all, I would NOT recommend this game. I don't see this becoming something incredible in the future, but I would love to see its ideas turned into something enjoyable and full.

[h1] Well, the game got updated. [/h1]
(this is gonna be long, I can feel it)
First things first, the game has undoubtebly improved in many areas, which is honestly quite commendable and straight up unexpected after the clusterfuck that were the two last updates (mainly the first one). As someone who tested this game way back in 2020, bought the game a while after, refunded it, then bought it again only to still be disappointed, I gotta say that this improvement is quite reassuring.
However, there are still a few things bugging me that make me lean more towards a not-recommended rather than a positive review, even though I would like to give it a neutral rating.

[h1] Guess I'll start off talking about what has been, in my opinion, improved: [/h1]

-Movement: Like seriously, movement was pretty good before, then it got annihilated with the Excessive update, and now its good again. It feels responsive and overall way more fun than the old movement we had.

-Gun models: They look pretty rad imo, and the inspect animations are just the icing on the cake (even if the lack of sounds when inspecting most guns is a bit of a bummer). Some of them as also still missing a secondary fire mode, which is a shame since it is one of this games most recognizable gunplay elements. But all in all, the guns feel good (At least the ones I was able to test, we'll get to that in a bit). I would also like to add that some reloads feel extremely long for a fast paced game like this, which breaks the flow of combat (this is only true for some weapons, like the heavy machinegun)
(+1 for keeping the workbench from the test branch btw, I really liked that addition.)

-Levels: They feature lootable containers, while I'm not a huge fan of the roguelite direction this game seems to be heading towards I do like having more stuff to do in the levels, the addition of vaults with workbenches and chests is also rather nice. Also that stupid parkour section at the start of every run is now gone, good riddance.

-Difficulty selector: It just looks cool man, love the little eye, such a handsome fella.

[h1] Now, for the negatives... [/h1]

-The door event: It's still there, unchanged from the last update as far as I can tell. I miss seeing the orange door, barreling towards it and simply going to the next level, because now you gotta do this discount Risk of Rain 2 event were you jump around like a madman trying to kill enough enemies to unlock the door and pass to the next level. It works for ROR2, it doesn't here. I get that some people may like it but an option to play using the legacy door system would be much appreciated.

Ingame Economy: It's really bad. You need to grind for so fucking long to unlock ONE extra gun for your character, and of course only for the duration of the run. Meaning that if you dont wanna get screwed by the game's ever increasing difficulty (another trait taken straight from ROR2) then I hope you like shooting that starter pistol because you'll be seeing it for a while, because a RANDOM GUN costs 900 crystals, and that takes a while to obtain, especially if you are planning on upgrading one of your guns or maybe getting a tactical/lethal equipment (Since you dont get ANYTHING by default, you really only have your pistol). Basically you get very little money and shit is too expensive, and getting new guns for your character is a chore and forces you to increase the threat level by farming relentlessly)

-Upgrade system / Roguelite focus: So, you wanted to hop in a game, shoot some baddies in an arena then hop off? Cool, there's like one unfinished arena and you get no reward for playing in it as far as I've seen. No money, no cards, no vines, nothing. If you want to actually get new loadouts and upgrades you are FORCED to play the roguelite mode (aka FPS ROR2 wannabe), which is not my cup of tea in this case (And I'm a huge fan of ROR2).
Instead of a casual shooter that you can quickly boot up to de-stress and quit when you feel like it, you're now stuck in this run that might take a good while to end. If you quit at any point you'll just go straight to the lobby and have to start over, so more grinding with the starter pistol.

-""Hidden mechanics"": It would be cool if the game told you about certain stuff straight away instead of making you look for it. Things like "this is where you have to go to select the arena mode", "this is how you obtain cards", "this is how you scan the area around you". As someone that has previously refunded the game, the first hour of the game is the most important thing for a new player since that's when they'll determine whether the game is worth keeping or not. If a player doesnt know how things work 1h into the game the chance of them refunding it only goes up. A few small popups would do this game wonders.

-Enemies/Combat: While most of the enemies are fine from a design perspective, the way they behave is sometimes extremely annoying, especially as the threat level goes up. They are relentless, constantly tailing your ass (that goes for EVERY enemy, even the ranged ones) when you want to regenerate health (which takes ages to start and ruins the combat flow). Seriously, some of these guys randomly hit you when you're going at 100km/h, which stops shield regen and forces you to play super passively again. Like give me some way of regenerating health while in combat, executions, combat rating DMC style, idk, just dont force me to hide or run away for what feels like 20 seconds waiting for my shields to come back. On another note, I personally felt that the enemies became really tanky really fast, so ammo goes down the drain really fast too.

-Unskippable death/revive animations: I know a lot of people have already complained about it, so I'm just adding my voice to that camp. Yeah we dont wanna see the same animation every time we die, and every time we come back to life, so please let us skip it.
An option to skip the upgrade altar would be nice too since we already have it at the base.

GTTOD is a game with a lot of potential. While it might be trying to ride the wave created by games like ghostrunner and neon white, among others, it has some unique features and it feels like it has the potential to be its own thing.

The problems start at the point where if you're the kind of player who seeks any actual polish, the current state of the game has little to none of it.

The movement is clunky, the momentum and inertia feel wrong, you get big burst of speeds you don't feel like you should get sometimes, the dash and wall run don't always work how you want (you have a setting for it, btw) and the maneuverability mid air is close to non existent especially at high speeds. You know, that "can't change my jump direction" feels. The level design is on the bland side, and there isn't much interesting tricks to pull off besides wall jumps left and right, and inconsistent dash resets.

The combat is complete chaos, but not really the good kind. You have a ton of enemies shooting in every direction, with very little visibility and clarity in general (be it the enemies or the actual environement), it's hard to figure out what's going, why you're taking damage from every directions, why you are still alive in spite of that. The weapons are so generous that it makes them matter very little, i can have a pistol, a shotgun or a bazooka, all i need to do is look in the general direction of enemies and they'll die. The bosses are no different, just run around hoping not to get hit and keep shooting toward the boss.

The levels quickly all become samey, even though there will be some randomizations and you can get random power ups throughout the runs which makes the gameplay have a bit of a roguelike flavor, but that's not enough to make it interesting imo.

So sure, if you're the kind of person who just wants to start up the game, go woosh HAYAHH woosh all over the place, and bang bang BOOOM explosions everywhere while killing everything, you might have fun, but personally i found it becoming stale really fast. If you're looking for more than just random chaos and you expect some depth, this ain't it yet. Thanksfully Early Access means there's a chance it'll get better.

I bought this game on sale, and just recently got to it after watching one of the creators dev vlogs. To be honest, there just doesn't seem to be a point in playing beyond the first 40 or so minutes at the moment.

GTTOD plays like a mashup of Risk of Rain/Muck, Doom/BPM, and somewhat, Ghost Runner.

The game has you rush to find the orange door at the end of each level. Once you find the door you must kill enemies to open said door to proceed to the next level. At the start of each level you can start a shrine that will spawn enemies that get progressively harder as you fight, but these enemy kills don't contribute to opening the door until you reach the door and activate it... they are only spawned to offer you a challenge and some money to buy guns or equipment. As a bonus, once you complete the level with the shrine activated you get some sort of randomized "Buff".

It sounds like a fun loop and the whole story idea of "Climbing to the top of a mountain" sounds awesome. But after playing 13 or so levels... that sense of "climbing to the top" just isn't clear. I fought a level 4 sentinel, and several levels later I fought a level 2 sentinel... why is the later enemy weaker? Am I making progress or am I not? The repeating level layouts didn't really help the case, so by that point I figured the game simply never ends because it is in Early access.

While guns, Gun slots, and equipment can be gotten fast enough (and are all mostly satisfying to use)...
Buff accrual is too slow in this game. Games like BPM, Muck, and Risk of Rain all had a pretty decent rate of Buff Accrual since you could pick up buffs from shrines or chests.

As the Early Access would let on, the game isn't ready for release. It needs work and the developer knows and is hilariously vocal about it in his lovely Dev VLogs on steam. I'm keeping this game to support the developer and because I look forward to seeing what this game can become, but my review will not be kept as "recommended" out of hope or pity. It will change to that when the game becomes more fleshed out and progression becomes more apparent.

Not the greatest game I've played. Very hard. Can't skip the tutorial in favor of game play. Cant even get past the tutorial and once you get into the combat phase of the tutorial and you die, it restarts. Can't skip cut scenes either.

Actual game is pretty fun, but there are a few things that hold it back. Namely, sloppy parkour and an un-skippable "warmup" before the actual game starts, every time. By sloppy parkour, I mean that the player's speed is often useless against enemies. With enough practice, you can go extremely fast, but the enemies are unable to keep up. Meaning that a lot of the time, you wallrun into an arena, kill one or two enemies in the air, and then are forced to sluggishly jump around on the ground in order to deal with the rest. Ground movement speed is also far too low. I get that you go faster in the air, but the speed at which the player walks is honestly just anti-fun garbage atm. Combine that with less than accurate wallrunning detection, buggy monkey bars and speed boosts, and a bugged door that doesn't work half the time and you have the worst part of the game, "the void". A parkour tutorial is fine, but it should be reserved for a help menu or the tutorial already present. Having to do the same 3-4 parkour layouts every time you start a run is awful for everyone. It's too difficult (and buggy) for new players, and irritating for experienced ones. Half the time you'll spend 10 minutes on the parkour and then close the game because of how bad the hit detection is. It's also worth mentioning that the maps are not randomly generated. Despite being a roguelike, the game has set levels that you'll have to go through every single time you play it. Set levels + unskippable buggy parkour = not very replayable. I really, really want to like this game, but atm, it's far too sluggish and irritating to fully recommend.

TLDR: Gunplay is fun, game looks great, but the parkour and unskippable tutorials make the game sluggish and a chore to play. I truly believe that the game will become better if given enough time, though.

TL;DR, infinitely squandered potential that grows ever more wasted. Massive gaps in updates, updates that have a tendency to remove, not add, content, and a potential upcoming paywall to test said very fickle updates. 

I bought this game back in 2019, and the amount of changes it has undergone is baffling. The issue is that the vast majority of them haven't been for the best, primarily when about half of the game's content was just outright scrapped after months of no updates, and then the game went several more months being untouched. 

The crux of my initial issue with this game came from the fact that it stopped being what I purchased in the first place, but I was excited for the development. 

Then after over a year, they re-add a lot of the cut content, but with worse mechanics. Then everything changes again, and this cycle pretty much just repeats. Radio silence, huge post about an update that isn't coming out for months, update comes out, repeat. 

After that very cycle has run its course again, the developer is now considering doing the popular thing of giving more game features to people who support them on patreon. That hasn't gone through yet, but considering their track record, it's probably going to happen. The Steam version gets zero attention, going month after month without any kind of update and then getting a massive dump of it and being shocked when things don't go great. Now, people will have to pay even more money to be able to see the game that they've already paid for get updated. 

Few games have conflicted me in such a guttural way, because I loved this game when I first picked it up. Many of its ideas were still unrealized, but its mechanics were smooth and the gameplay loop was tight. Those mechanics were then progressively made worse over the course of many months and far fewer updates. The game has undergone numerous shifts in gameplay and feel since I started following it, and rarely has it been for the best. At its most recent peak, the game has felt about as stable as it did when I first played over a year ago. Wall running, the HUD, and weapons all kept getting changed, and each time the game got less inspired. Wall running got worse, the HUD just ripped of Halo, and half the guns also followed the HUD and became Halo 5's arsenal. I just don't understand this game or its development cycle. The issue with having such a skewed image of your creative child is when you 1) Charge money for it 2) Have zero intent on consulting your large player base. 

That second issue is made all the worse considering they'll only be listening to feedback from people willing to pay m o r e money. They claim to have cancelled their Patreon previously because they felt like they had nothing to give, but after this much time of ignoring their struggling player base, having a paywall on feedback is just abhorrent. 

Most of what happens behind the scenes with this game just makes zero sense. It's a genuine shame to see such potential wasted, especially when so much time and passion has gone into it. It's just a tragedy that most of the time was spent avoiding feedback like it were the plague.

Guns and movement feel pretty good, but enemies and level design are basically awful and make the game unplayable. 

Just on a basic fundamental level the enemies are badly modeled, designed, and implemented. For starters enemies have hitboxes that range from 2-3 times their actual model, which becomes very bizarre to aim at AIR 5 meters away from something and still hit targets. Normally hitboxes are larger than models to account for jank movement, but this is just out of line. Besides hitboxes being totally out of wack with their models, the actual models themselves are just some bright glowing lines. This would be very cool, if enemies didn't bunch together and create an incomprehensible mass of glowing zigzags. Differentiating enemies even when they are separate is rather annoying, but in a group I don't even know what the hell I'm firing at most of the time. Not that it really matters though, none of the enemies really add anything to the gameplay. Melee enemies might as well not exist since you will be in the air for 99% of the time, and the ranged enemies lack the depth that strafe shooters like Serious Sam has. The absolute worst enemy design though is this mech(I think its a mech?) that fires from what I understand to be as homing 0 counterplay missiles. The only "counter" to them I found was breaking LOS and then waiting for shields to recharge before getting back in LOS so I can shoot them down. Assuming of course - I can even see the glowing outline of the mech in a sea of other glowing lines.

The level design is just strange, its sometimes vertical - but without fast ways to go up and enemies have no way to follow you quickly if you drop down anyways. Despite the advanced movement system, the layout of the environment is so spaced apart and open that much of the time you are just gliding through the air instead of interacting with anything. You may think being open leads to more freedom, but instead you are often just following whatever giant wall pattern was placed by the devs since there is literally nothing else to use. Not to mention that moving throughout the level feels counter-intuitive to killing enemies since by the time they spawn in, you would have already soared past them many times over. The way spawns work is that the game wants you to fight them in that set location, I'm assuming because they have no way to follow you or keep up. This means you will basically just run back and forth over and over again in a big hallway while killing enemies, instead of being able to just run around the map wherever you want and shooting when you have a shot or feel like it.

Beyond those two massive failings what does the game offer? A bugged out portal every 15 minutes forcing you to restart? Completely unfinished "hub" area with nothing in it that you have to wonder why its even in the public release? Nonexistance story? The reality is that there is nothing to play here, if you want to go fast and kill stuff then play Ultrakill, Cloudbuilt, Ghostrunner, Nu-Doom, Titanfall, etc. This game should not be on the store for anything besides free.

I want to genuinely review this game, and I know just as damn well as the next person that 3 hours is not a lot to go off of, but hear me out here. This game is early access, yes, but it doesn't feel like early access. It feels like a prototype, or a proof of concept. This is like the base for a game that devs make first, and then spend months, or even years, building on top of.

I'm not going to add my opinions about all the potential it has, because anyone who knows anything about this game knows that it has been nothing but a ball of potential since it came out. But that potential evidently hasn't gone anywhere. I waited for the last update to get this game because I knew that if I didn't, I'd be playing a very bare-bones game. Now that the game has more to it, it still feels so very far from complete.

Let's talk mechanics. Movement is stiff. Dashing, wall running, and slide hopping are the b̶e̶s̶t̶ only ways to get around quickly, yet they're all so buggy or janky. It's hard to tell what walls can and cannot be used to run on, dashing is more of a light dodge with no momentum gains, and slide hopping is difficult due to constant clipping on uneven terrain and depth perception/animation issues. On top of that, the ground can be really, REALLY hard to see sometimes, due to poor lighting. The cyberpunk aesthetic has gone too far if I can't tell how far I am from the ground under me. As far as the randomizer mechanics go, I can't really judge without enough experience, but it seems to me that all that gets changed is the insides of bunkers and dungeons.

The graphics are a serious concern of mine. Since the ground isn't always properly visible (or distinguishable from the walls), depth is not always present. Enemies and their attacks are all the same colors, be it yellow or grey, and in large groups, it becomes extremely difficult to pick out exactly what enemy you are looking at. Names don't help either, since enemies are almost always jumbled together, and some names are just too similar to distinguish at a glance. I'd hate to tell the devs what to do, but visual clarity needs to be achieved. I'm not sure the synth-cyberpunk aesthetic is a good fit for the game in the first place, but since it's here, it needs to be taken advantage of. Enemies need to be distinct, and attacks need to be clear and concise. Also, more of a nitpick in comparison, but visual variety would be greatly appreciated. The same dilapidated roads and floating crystal islands get old REALLY fast.

Combat is probably my biggest criticism. The game doesn't really give you the time to learn your enemies individually. Arguably, this should be overlooked, as the game is a rogue like, but to throw new players into an arena with several different types of similarly colored enemies all engaging in different ways does nothing but encourage the player to kite and learn crowd control. As more enemies are introduced, the kiting becomes more akin to fleeing, and the player's ability to control the mess in front of (or behind) them disappears. Learning the game is just not intuitive this way. Doable, yes, but not intuitive.

My experience with this game has been frantic, fast paced jank. I have met more bugs than I think fair for 3 hours, and I really can't recommend this game in it's current state. I will, of course, update this as I play more and as updates come out, but right now, I can't say this game is really worth full price. Get it on sale if you're really interested.

[h1]Rating[/h1]
3/10

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Good grief, it's actually staggering just how different the game is in its current state, when compared to the demo I played. If that's not false advertising, I don't know what is. Whereas the demo encourages getting up close and personal with the enemies, the Early Access release punishes you for taking that approach with a swift death. Speaking of death, it's another one of those Rogue-likes, that wears unfair deaths on its sleeve. Because of course it does. Needless to say, of you want a great movement shooter, go play Titanfall 2 instead. If you want a great Rogue-like shooter, go play Mullet Mad Jack instead.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
+ Good soundtrack.
+ Good enemy variety.
+ Good weapon variety.
+ Weapons have great impact.
+ Good aesthetics and graphics.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
- Reduced health amount discourages aggressive play unlike the demo. I found myself running away from enemies, more so than engaging them, because of this change.
- Movement has been stiffened when compared to the demo. It's hard to describe in words, other than your momentum seems to just stop, the moment you jump off a wall.
- No permanent upgrade tree to upgrade your character's stats between runs. Which wouldn't have been an issue, if your character didn't feel so under-powered to begin with.
- Levels don't seem to be randomised with each run. Usually Rogue-likes would randomise levels, as a means to keep each run fresh or at least try to. But that simply isn't here for some reason.

another issue is the art direction. while it is good, and is visually pleasing, incorporating it into the enemy designs makes it near impossible to tell enemies apart from one another, as well as making it difficult to discern what enemy does what. it all becomes a bit orange yellow glowing mess once a few minutes have passed, making it hard to judge what is a priority target amongst the horde. Which leads into my next point, the weapons presented to you, especially in the early game, do NOT clear the hordes well. youre stuck with weapons that are primarily single target, while youre put up against 30-40 enemies as early on as the first stage. theres no real satisfaction to slowly chipping away at one enemy's hp bar, just for 3 more to spawn behind it as soon as you take it. when i saw this game, i assumed it was a fun game to clear out hordes with with lots of weapons, but it felt hard to enjoy that power trip with the lackluster early game. 

some final issues i have are the crosshair not being customizeable (especially considering how bad the default one is) the enemy hitboxes being absurdly small (the lack of bullet tracers also makes this annoying, due to you sometimes having your crosshair right over an enemy and the shot missing) and the overall lack of a clear goal, (should i sprint for the door right away? should i loot some more? do i kill some enemies?) 

all in all, the game has potential, but needs to figure out what it wants to be rather than trying to combine too many different elements without explaining them well enough. ill definitely keep an eye on it for future updates, and the eventual release, but in its current state, i cant really recommend it due to the lack of clear vision of what it wants to be, and what it wants you to do.
